blocks.text: Data parallelism splits a large batch across multiple devices, each holding a full copy of the model, computing gradients independently on its own portion of the batch, then synchronizing those gradients together before applying one combined weight update.

It is the simplest and most widely used form of distributed training, and this topic covers its mechanics in depth, building on the brief overview covered in the earlier Training Infrastructure module.
1. What Data Parallelism Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102652-839003327.png

Rather than processing an entire batch on a single device, data parallelism divides that batch into smaller chunks, one per available device, letting several devices work through different portions of the same batch simultaneously.
2. Each Device Holds a Full Model Copy

blocks.alt: Each Device Holds a Full Model Copy
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102652-714463860.png

In standard data parallelism, every participating device maintains its own complete copy of the model weights, meaning the model itself must fully fit on each individual device, a constraint that becomes important later in this module when comparing against techniques that split the model itself.
3. Synchronizing Gradients Across Devices
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102652-443235286.png

After each device computes gradients using its own portion of the batch, those gradients get synchronized and averaged across all participating devices, so every device ends up applying the exact same combined weight update, keeping all model copies identical throughout training.

code.content:
# A conceptual sketch of data parallel training
local_gradients = compute_gradients(model, local_batch_portion)
averaged_gradients = all_reduce_average(local_gradients, across="all_devices")
apply_update(model, averaged_gradients)

blocks.text: 4. Data Parallelism and Effective Batch Size

blocks.alt: Data Parallelism and Effective Batch Size
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102652-799524312.png

The effective batch size under data parallelism equals the number of participating devices multiplied by the batch size each device processes individually, similar in spirit to how gradient accumulation, covered in the Training Fundamentals module, achieves a larger effective batch size, but through parallel devices rather than sequential accumulation steps.
5. Communication Overhead in Data Parallelism
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102652-428687193.png

Synchronizing gradients across devices requires real network communication, and as the number of devices grows, this synchronization step can become a meaningful source of overhead, particularly if the network connecting the devices is slower than the computation happening on each one.
6. Data Parallelism's Memory Limitation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102652-746926322.png

Because every device needs a full model copy, data parallelism alone does not help if the model itself is too large to fit on a single device, that specific problem is what model parallelism, tensor parallelism, and the ZeRO techniques covered later in this module are designed to address instead.

blocks.title: This is exactly why this module covers several distinct parallelism strategies
blocks.content: Data parallelism solves the problem of processing more data faster, while model parallelism and its variants solve the different problem of fitting a model that is simply too large for one device, and real training setups often combine both.

blocks.text: 7. Data Parallelism vs Gradient Accumulation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472102883-385092221.png

Data parallelism achieves a larger effective batch size by running several devices in parallel, while gradient accumulation, covered in the Training Fundamentals module, achieves the same goal sequentially on a single device, the two techniques can also be combined together when both multiple devices and memory constraints are in play.
8. When Data Parallelism Is the Right Fit

Data parallelism is the right fit specifically when the model comfortably fits on a single device but training would benefit from processing more data faster using multiple devices, the most common distributed training scenario for fine-tuning projects that have access to more than one GPU.
9. Data Parallelism as the Foundation for More Advanced Techniques

Understanding data parallelism clearly is essential groundwork for the more advanced sharding techniques, FSDP and the ZeRO stages, covered later in this module, since those techniques build directly on the data parallel idea while additionally addressing its full model copy memory limitation.
Worked Example

A team with access to four GPUs, each capable of holding their fine-tuning model comfortably, uses data parallelism to split their training batch across all four devices, each processing a quarter of the batch and computing its own gradients before synchronizing.

Their effective batch size grows fourfold compared to using a single device, and their training completes proportionally faster, since all four devices work simultaneously, a direct, straightforward benefit from data parallelism given their model already fit comfortably on each individual device.
Common Mistakes

items: Attempting data parallelism for a model too large to fit on a single device, when a different parallelism strategy is actually needed
Underestimating gradient synchronization overhead when scaling to a large number of devices with a slow network connection
Confusing data parallelism, which splits the batch, with model parallelism, which splits the model itself
Not accounting for the increased effective batch size when tuning learning rate and other hyperparameters under data parallelism

blocks.text: Practice

For a training setup with a chosen number of devices and a per-device batch size, calculate the resulting effective batch size, and consider how that might affect learning rate choices covered in the Training Fundamentals module.
Key Takeaway

Data parallelism splits a training batch across multiple devices, each holding a full model copy, computing gradients independently before synchronizing them into one combined update, a straightforward way to speed up training and increase effective batch size, though it requires the model itself to comfortably fit on each individual device.
